clue.text: Produces hat after giving outstanding performance

parts.note: a producer who stages something shows it
a top hat is a topper

explanation.surface: A magician pulls something from a hat after a stunning act.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a conjuror; 'after giving' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A turn so good the audience's applause halts the show is the theatre's term for a triumph.

clue.text: Determined attack

definitions.meaning: to be set on or bent on doing something is to be resolved to do it
to fall on someone violently, to assail them

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to be resolved on a course and to assail someone, as a gang might.

clue.text: Decorated knight coming in to make a speech

indicators.note: the knight's letter enters the middle of the speech-making verb

parts.note: to orate is to deliver a formal speech
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A newly honoured knight arrives to give an address.
explanation.definitionFit: Something highly decorated is elaborately adorned, a synonym of ornamented.

clue.text: Workout garments — father wearing set wasn't relaxed

indicators.note: the scrambled letters put father on, so he sits inside them
the letters of the two words are loosened into a new order

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A dad squeezed into gym kit, and the team that saw him was tense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wasn't relaxed' reads as one phrase, but 'relaxed' alone rearranges SET WASN'T into SWEATNTS, and 'wearing' puts PA inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose trousers worn for exercise are the clothing named, so they fit gym wear.

clue.text: Spherical objects in old Scottish bank

parts.note: RBS is the Royal Bank of Scotland

explanation.surface: Round items found in the vaults of a historic Scottish bank.
explanation.walkthrough: RBS is the Royal Bank of Scotland, a major British high-street bank.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball or globe is a round thing, the plain sense of the plural noun.

clue.text: Extremely painful, drastic action, not physical

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters
drastic action is violent, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: Severe pain prompts drastic measures, though nothing physical is involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' takes PL from the ends of 'painful'; 'drastic' rearranges ACTION into ATONIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Love or friendship without a sexual element is described this way, after Plato.

clue.text: Conductor on top of double-decker, flustered

indicators.note: in a down answer the first piece sits on the second

parts.note: Sir Simon Rattle is a famous orchestral conductor

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down entry is its first letter

explanation.surface: A bus conductor up on the top deck of a double-decker, looking flustered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests a bus conductor, but it is Simon Rattle of the orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone put off balance and nervous is unsettled, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: English king about to join returning train

indicators.note: the whole assembly is read backwards
the royal letters go round the joining verb

parts.note: ER stands for a king or queen of England, Rex or Regina
to unite is to join together

explanation.surface: An English monarch is about to board a train heading home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'train' is not a railway but a following; 'about' wraps the joining verb in the royal letters to make EUNITER, which 'returning' reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: A train is a body of attendants following an important person, as in a royal entourage.

clue.text: In Berkshire town, fell over in part of library

parts.note: Reading is a large town in Berkshire, west of London

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the word is turned upside down

parts.note: a fell is upland moor in northern England

explanation.surface: Someone tripped and fell over in a town's library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fell' looks like a verb but is the noun for a hill or moor; 'over' reverses MOOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A quiet area set aside for study in a library is the named space.

clue.text: Lucky dip bishop organised, only with backing

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
to run an event is to organise it

indicators.note: backing means the word is written backwards

parts.note: but can mean only, as in 'but a child'

explanation.surface: A bishop set up the church fete's lucky dip, with only modest support.
explanation.walkthrough: A lucky dip is a British fair game where you rummage in a tub for a hidden prize.
explanation.definitionFit: A tub filled with bran hiding prizes is the traditional form of the game of chance.

clue.text: Film policeman saving good man holding on

indicators.note: the policeman keeps good safe inside

parts.note: busy is old British slang for a police officer

indicators.note: the man holds the second word within

parts.note: male is used for a man

explanation.surface: In a movie, a cop rescues a decent man who is clinging on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'busy' is old British slang for a policeman; 'saving' and 'holding' are both containment signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Parker's 1976 gangster musical with a cast of children is the named movie.

clue.text: A beginner in patisserie with very little desire for food

indicators.note: the beginner of a word is its first letter

parts.note: petite means small and dainty

explanation.surface: A novice at a pastry shop has only a tiny hunger.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunger, the wish to eat, is the plain meaning of the noun.

clue.text: Trouble on golf hole that bends sharply

parts.note: to dog someone is to trouble or pester them
leg is the on side in cricket, the side the batsman stands at

explanation.surface: A golfer runs into trouble on an awkward hole.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the leg side is also called the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairway with an abrupt angle, like a dog's hind leg, is the golfer's term for it.

clue.text: Chief minister given opportunity to turn up

parts.note: a chance is an opportunity

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to roll is to turn over

explanation.surface: A leading minister is offered the chance to show up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn up' looks like a phrasal verb, but 'turn' gives ROLL and 'up' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Germany and Austria the head of government holds this title, a chief minister.

clue.text: Centre for missionaries?

indicators.note: the centre of the word is its middle four letters, with four either side

explanation.surface: A query about where a mission was based.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre' suggests an office or building, but it takes the middle of 'missionaries', and the whole clue also describes the Scottish island where St Columba founded his abbey.
explanation.definitionFit: St Columba's abbey on this Hebridean island was the base for evangelising Scotland and northern England.

clue.text: A dreadful shock this time when everything goes wrong?

parts.note: bad means dreadful
a shock of hair is a thick mass of it
a day is a period of time

explanation.surface: A terrible fright this time, on one of those days when nothing goes right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shock' suggests a fright but is the thick mop of hair; the question mark flags that the first reading is playful.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a day on which nothing goes right, beginning with unruly hair.

clue.text: Experienced soldier about to finish with TA causes feud

indicators.note: the soldier's letters go around the finishing word

parts.note: a vet, short for veteran, is an experienced soldier
to end is to finish

explanation.surface: An old soldier, about to wind up his service with the Territorial Army, starts a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force; 'about' is a containment signal, not 'about to'.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-running bitter quarrel between families is a blood feud.

clue.text: Memorial in Verona gets vandalised

indicators.note: vandalised things are smashed up, so the letters are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: A monument in the Italian city of Verona is defaced.
explanation.definitionFit: A stone marker on a grave commemorates the dead, so it is a memorial.

clue.text: One failing to gain a place in American orchestra carried on

definitions.text: One failing to gain a place

parts.note: LSO is the London Symphony Orchestra
to run is to carry on or continue

explanation.surface: An American orchestra kept playing in the competition.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'place' in racing means finishing in the first three.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse finishing outside the placings is the racing term for an unsuccessful runner.

clue.text: Fine artist points to lady's fingers

parts.note: OK means fine or satisfactory
RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A painter gestures towards a woman's elegant fingers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lady's fingers' looks like a body part but is the vegetable's other name.
explanation.definitionFit: The green seed pods eaten as a vegetable are also called ladies' fingers from their slender shape.

clue.text: Part of criminal law on kidnap upset wise guy

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means the run is turned upside down
a part of these words is a run of their letters

explanation.surface: Some kidnap legislation is overturned by a clever lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' takes LLAWONK from 'criminal law on kidnap'; 'upset' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart alec who acts as if he has every answer is a wise guy in the ironic sense.

clue.text: Make pale ale somehow in British church

indicators.note: the rearranged beer letters go inside the two abbreviations
somehow means the letters are arranged in some other way

explanation.surface: Pale ale somehow ends up in a British church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pale' in the surface describes the beer, but the definition is 'Make pale'; 'somehow' gives LEA, which 'in' places inside the abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: To whiten or remove colour with chemicals is to make something lighter.

clue.text: In contact with team working towards the same goal

parts.note: on means touching, as a cup on a table
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: Keeping in touch with a team that pulls together.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on side means supporting a shared aim, in agreement with colleagues.

clue.text: Right bother rolling in it

parts.note: well, as in 'all well', means right or fine
a to-do is a fuss or bother

explanation.surface: Real trouble from someone who is very rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right bother' reads like British slang for 'real trouble'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being rolling in it is an idiom for having plenty of money, so wealthy.

clue.text: Pleased, statesman having lost weight

indicators.note: the weight is taken away from the statesman's name

parts.note: William Gladstone was a Victorian Prime Minister
a stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A politician is delighted to have slimmed down.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of body weight, 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling happy about something is a simple synonym for being delighted.

clue.text: Altar? I'm fearful of marriage

indicators.note: a fearful person is shaken up, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A nervous person facing the altar admits being scared of wedlock.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to matrimony, as in wedded vows or wedded bliss.

clue.text: Possible problem with pipes in a lake running by edges of Grasmere

indicators.note: running water moves about, so the letters are shifted
the edges of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A plumbing fault in the Lake District beside Grasmere.
explanation.walkthrough: Grasmere is a village and lake in England's Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: Escaping water from a cracked or faulty tube is a familiar plumbing problem.

clue.text: The eland ran nervously out of the ark

indicators.note: the antelope moves jumpily, so its letters are shaken up

explanation.surface: An antelope ran skittishly out of Noah's ark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of the ark' looks like Noah's animals leaving; it means hopelessly old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Something out of the Ark is outdated; a primitive caveman type is the epitome of being behind the times.
